## Introduction

Welcome! In this module, we are going to learn how to build maps in R. While you are likely familiar with using `ggplot2` to make scatterplots and bar charts, mapping requires handling a special type of data: **spatial vectors** (points, lines, and polygons).

By the end of this worksheet, you will know how to take a standard dataset of bird sightings (latitude and longitude), convert it into spatial data, and layer it over real-world political and physical boundaries.

## 1. The Spatial Toolkit: Beyond the Tidyverse

To map data, we need libraries that understand geography. We will load `tidyverse` for our standard data wrangling, alongside these spatial-specific packages:

-   **`sf` (Simple Features):** The backbone of spatial analysis in R. It allows R to treat geographic shapes (like the boundary of New York or the exact point a hawk was seen) as standard dataframe columns.
-   **`tigris`:** A package that connects directly to the US Census Bureau to download state, county, and regional boundaries.
-   **`rnaturalearth`:** Great for global physical features, like oceans, major lakes, or country borders.
-   **`ggrepel`:** An extension for `ggplot2` that pushes text labels away from each other so they don't overlap on your map.

```{r load-libraries}
# You may need to have them run install.packages("rinat") in the console first!
# install.packages("rinat")
library(rinat)

# Load the necessary libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)         
library(rnaturalearth)  
library(ggrepel)
```

## 2. Setting the Stage: Getting Base Maps

Before we can plot our birds, we need a map for them to sit on. We will fetch the political boundaries for the Northeastern US using `tigris`, the Canadian provinces using `rnaturalearth`, and the physical boundary of the Atlantic Ocean.

```{r get-base-maps}

# 1. Fetch US state boundaries using the tigris package
ne_states <- states(
  # cb = TRUE downloads "Cartographic Boundaries". 
  # This gives us smoothed lines made for visual mapping, rather than highly 
  # detailed legal boundaries (which often extend far out into the ocean!).
  cb = TRUE, 
  
  # resolution = "500k" sets the detail level to a 1:500,000 scale. 
  # This is a great balance: it looks detailed but keeps the map rendering fast.
  resolution = "500k"
) %>% 
  # STUSPS is the column in the tigris data holding the 2-letter state postal code
  filter(STUSPS %in% c("NY", "PA", "NJ", "CT", "MA", "VT", "NH", "ME", "RI"))


# 2. Fetch Canadian provinces using rnaturalearth
# Since our map extends north, we need land for the Canadian birds to sit on!
canada_prov <- ne_states(
  country = "canada", 
  returnclass = "sf"
)


# 3. Fetch a physical map of the ocean from the Natural Earth database
ocean_base <- ne_download(
  # scale = 50 gives us a medium resolution map (1:50 million).
  scale = 50, 
  
  # category and type tell the database exactly what physical feature we want to download.
  category = "physical", 
  type = "ocean", 
  
  # returnclass = "sf" is CRITICAL! It forces R to return the data as a modern 
  # "simple feature" spatial object that works perfectly with ggplot2.
  returnclass = "sf"
)

```

> **Pro-Tip for Future Projects:** You can change `STUSPS` to any state abbreviation to map different regions, or use `rnaturalearth::ne_countries()` if you are mapping bird migrations internationally!
>
> **Watch out for `cb = TRUE`:** If you ever map coastal birds and set `cb = FALSE` in tigris, R will draw the state polygons extending miles out into the Atlantic Ocean (to the legal maritime borders), which covers up the coastal geography!

## 3. Fetch live, real Red-tailed Hawk sightings from iNaturalist

This grabs recent citizen science observations directly from the web.

```{r hawk_data}
hawk_data <- get_inat_obs(
  taxon_name = "Buteo jamaicensis", # Red-tailed Hawk
  
  # Set a geographic bounding box: c(min_lat, min_lon, max_lat, max_lon)
  # This matches the Northeast US and parts of Southeastern Canada
  bounds = c(38, -81, 48, -66),     
  
  # Limit the results so the API downloads quickly in a classroom setting
  maxresults = 700                  
)
```

## 4. Convert standard dataframe into a spatial (sf) object

```{r make-spatial}
hawks_sf <- st_as_sf(
  hawk_data, 
  
  # iNaturalist returns coordinate columns named exactly "longitude" and "latitude"
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), 
  
  # EPSG code 4326 means standard WGS84 GPS coordinates
  crs = 4326
)              
```

## 5. Layering the Map with `ggplot2`



Now that all our spatial objects share the same CRS, we build the map exactly like a standard `ggplot`. Think of it like a layer cake: we add layers from bottom to top using `geom_sf()`. `geom_sf()` is incredibly smart—it automatically figures out if it's drawing polygons (states/provinces) or points (birds).

```{r build-base-map}
hawk_map <- ggplot() +
  
  # Layer 1: The Ocean (Bottom layer)
  geom_sf(data = ocean_base, fill = "aliceblue", color = NA) +
  
  # Layer 2: Canada (Middle layer, landmass)
  geom_sf(data = canada_prov, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  
  # Layer 3: The US States (Middle layer, landmass)
  geom_sf(data = ne_states, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  
  # Layer 4: The Birds! (Top layer)
  # Since every row is one sighting, we just set a static size and color.
  # alpha = 0.5 makes the dots slightly transparent so we can see where sightings cluster!
  geom_sf(data = hawks_sf, color = "darkred", size = 1.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  
  # Zooming the map: Crop the "camera" to just the Northeast US / SE Canada bounding box
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-81, -66), ylim = c(38, 48)) +
  
  theme_minimal()

# Let's take a look at our progress
hawk_map
```

Finally, we can save our masterpiece for a report or presentation!

```{r export-map}
#| eval: false

# ggsave automatically saves the last plot displayed (or the one you specify).
# Setting exact widths and heights ensures your text and points scale properly.
ggsave("hawk_distribution_map.pdf", plot = hawk_map, width = 7, height = 6, units = "in")
```
